html:
The Baniwa, who call themselves Walimanai, are an Arawakan-speaking people of the Içana River and its tributaries in the northwest Amazon, where Brazil, Colombia and Venezuela meet. They are close kin of the Kurripako.

They live in riverside villages, farm bitter manioc, fish and hunt. Baniwa baskets woven from arumã fibre are known across Brazil. They take part in the wider exchange of the upper Rio Negro with peoples such as the Tariana, the Warekena and the Cubeo.

The rubber boom brought forced labour to the Içana in the late 1800s. In the mid 1900s evangelical missionaries converted many Baniwa. Most live in Brazil today.
